claims.text: Creep resistance in FCC/BCC HEA protective coatings is primarily governed by uniformly distributed coherent nanoscale precipitates at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Secondary phases or precipitates can preferentially occur at microstructural boundaries in HEAs.
The as-deposited coating has a heterogeneous microstructure and a nonuniform precipitate distribution.
Tailored heat treatment will nucleate and uniformly disperse coherent B2 or L1₂ nanoscale precipitates at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Coherent interphase precipitates act as pinning sites for dislocations.
The interphase precipitates impede dislocation climb.
The interphase precipitates impede grain-boundary sliding.
Interphase precipitates raise the local activation energy for dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding.
Suppressing dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding reduces the coating's creep rate during continuous loading.
The heat-treated coating will have a significantly lower creep rate than the as-deposited coating.
The heat-treated coating will have a higher creep activation energy than the as-deposited coating.
The heat-treated coating will have a longer time to failure than the as-deposited coating.
Weak phase-boundary pinning in the as-deposited coating causes a higher creep rate.
Elevated temperature and sustained applied stress are conditions under which HEA creep can be measured.
Dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding dominate deformation throughout the proposed high-temperature, high-stress operating regime.
The optimal precipitate size, spacing, and coherency may depend on alloy composition and test conditions.
